I know it's a contentious topic, but I just finished this novel and adored it. As messed up and twisted as it was, Nabokov is a masterful painter of the wretched American tourist landscape, and he captures perfectly the neurotic, self-absorbed/deluded Humbert as he's holding poor Dolores captive in more ways than one. And those little nuggets of rebellion and sadness we saw of her---god, my heart ripped.

And his language? Sweet mercy. More than half of his vocabulary was so Latin, my dictionary didn't even have it. Luckily I knew enough Romance to parse the occasional French snippet that shows up here or there, too, which definitely supplemented the experience.

The metaphors and masterful weaving of his words were just... they were like a dazzling tapestry, woven out of other, smaller tapestries. A fractal masterpiece.

I thought it was tedious and I didn't care that it was deliberate and reflecting the character of Humbert Humbert. I didn't find anything in it amusing, even things like Humbert's mother being killed by lightning. I challenge anyone to quote a funny a supposedly literary bit in it, since clearly the point is Humbert is a pretentious monster trying to cover his shitty nature behind pseduoart.

I loved the novel for some of the reasons you mentioned. The language is so amazing that I found it a pleasure to read large blocks of the story aloud. His descriptions of America on the road are some of the best and funniest parts of the story, too.

The books importance stems from Nabokov's decision to write about a taboo subject with sympathy, delicacy, and humor. It is because Humbert is so brazen, so pompous, so full of himself, that he comes across as so funny. I can't adequately explain why but his over the top intelligence and the contempt he holds for so many, including his reader at some points, makes me laugh.

Of course, much of this is lost in Stanley Kubrick's version of the film, and even he admitted that he had a difficult time bringing it to screen since so much of the novel's pleasure comes from the language and Nabokov's style. It is another example of where the novel far surpasses the film.
